Philippians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

The Philippian believers cared deeply about the apostle Paul.

Paul wrote to strengthen their faith, encourage them to live in a manner worthy of Christ's gospel, warn them against teachers who wanted to impose Jewish practices, and express gratitude for their generosity and Christian kindness.

Henry describes this as the only one of Paul's letters containing no explicit or implied rebuke.

Instead, every part displays Paul's praise and confidence in the Philippians.

He addresses them with a particular warmth and affection that any attentive reader can recognize.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle offers up thanksgivings and prayers, for the good work of grace in the Philippians.1–7He expresses affection, and prays for them.8–11Fortifies them against being cast down at his sufferings.12–20He stood prepared for glorifying Christ by life, or death.21–26Exhortations to zeal, and constancy in professing the gospel.27–30
Thanksgiving for God's work among the Philippians (verses 1–7)

The greatest honor of even the most distinguished minister is to be a servant of Jesus Christ.

Those who are not genuinely saints here on earth will never become saints in heaven.

Apart from Christ, even the best believers remain sinners, unable to stand before a holy God.

There is no genuine peace without grace.

True inward peace grows from knowing God's favor.

And all grace and peace originate with God our Father, the fountain of every blessing.

Paul had been badly treated at Philippi and had seen relatively little immediate fruit from his efforts.

Yet he remembered the believers there with joy.

We should thank God when other Christians grow in grace, receive comfort, develop gifts or become useful servants.

We benefit through their growth, and God receives the glory.

The work of divine grace will not reach perfection until the day when Jesus Christ appears.

Yet we may be confident that God will complete every genuine work of salvation he has begun through regeneration.

That confidence must not rest upon outward appearances, but upon evidence of a new creation leading to holiness.

Believers grow especially dear to the ministers through whose service they have received spiritual help.

Those who suffer together for God's cause should likewise hold one another dear.

Paul prays for growing love and discernment (verses 8–11)

Should we not love and show compassion to the people whom Christ loves and pities?

No one possesses so much of a grace that no further growth is needed.

Paul wanted the believers to recognize differences and choose what is most excellent.

Christ's truths and commands really are excellent.

They reveal their excellence to an attentive mind.

Sincerity should govern our behavior and is an ornament to all Christian graces.

Believers should not be quick to take offense.

They should be especially careful not to offend God or one another.

What brings God the greatest honor also brings us the greatest good.

We should not leave it doubtful whether our lives bear any spiritual fruit.

A small amount of Christian love, discernment and fruitful service should never satisfy us.

Paul's imprisonment advances the gospel (verses 12–20)

Paul wrote while a prisoner in Rome.

He wanted the Philippians not to be discouraged or ashamed of his suffering for Christ.

God's wisdom and goodness had turned his imprisonment into a means of advancing the gospel.

People who would otherwise never have known Paul or heard the message now learned about him and began asking questions.

Paul was troubled not only by enemies but also by supposed friends who preached Christ out of envy and rivalry, hoping to make his imprisonment harder.

What a miserable attitude toward a faithful servant of God!

Yet Paul remained composed and joyful.

If our troubles lead to blessings for other people, we should take comfort and even rejoice.

Every experience that contributes to our salvation does so through the Spirit of Jesus Christ.

Prayer is the means God has appointed for seeking that help.

Our highest ambition should not be to win human applause or escape the cross.

We should hope to remain faithful under temptation, contempt and suffering.

Let Christ decide how we can best serve his glory.

He may use us through hard work or suffering, through diligence or patience, by our living to honor him or even by our dying in his service.

To live is Christ; to die is gain (verses 21–26)

For a person who lives only for this world, death is great loss.

That person loses earthly pleasures, possessions and hopes.

But for a genuine believer, death is gain.

It ends remaining weakness and misery, delivers the believer from the troubles of life and brings the soul into possession of the highest good: Christ himself.

Paul's difficult choice was not whether earthly existence was better than heaven.

There is no comparison between those two conditions.

His struggle was between two good things: serving Christ here or enjoying Christ's presence in heaven.

Faith and divine grace can make believers willing to die.

On earth we continue struggling against sin.

With Christ, we will be free forever from sin, temptation, grief and death.

Nevertheless, those who have the strongest reason to desire heaven should remain willing to live and serve as long as God still has work for them.

When God gives mercies we did not expect, his providential hand becomes especially evident in them.

Live as citizens worthy of the gospel (verses 27–30)

People who profess Christ's gospel should behave like those who believe its teachings, submit to its commands and rely upon its promises.

The word translated conduct or conversation originally evokes the life of citizens who seek their city's honor, peace, safety and prosperity.

The gospel contains truths so valuable that they are worth struggling to defend and practice.

Opposition is real, and we must persevere.

People may drift carelessly toward destruction.

Those seeking heaven must remain watchful and diligent.

Christians can enjoy unity of heart and affection even when they differ in judgment on many lesser matters.

Faith is God's gift for Christ's sake.

The ability and willingness to trust him come from God.

If we suffer disgrace or loss for Christ's sake, we should also regard that opportunity as a gift.

But the bodily suffering itself does not earn salvation.

Persecution is not meritorious.

Our salvation comes from God alone, and both faith and patience are his gracious gifts.
classic_reading:
[Phil.1.1-Phil.1.7]
Philippians
The Philippians felt a very deep interest for the apostle. The scope of the epistle is to confirm them in the faith, to encourage them to walk as becomes the gospel of Christ, to caution them against judaizing teachers, and to express gratitude for their Christian bounty. This epistle is the only one, among those written by St. Paul, in which no censures are implied or expressed. Full commendation and confidence are in every part, and the Philippians are addressed with a peculiar affection, which every serious reader will perceive.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The apostle offers up thanksgivings and prayers, for the good work of grace in the Philippians. | (1-7) |
He expresses affection, and prays for them. | (8-11) |
Fortifies them against being cast down at his sufferings. | (12-20) |
He stood prepared for glorifying Christ by life, or death. | (21-26) |
Exhortations to zeal, and constancy in professing the gospel. | (27-30) |
Verses 1-7
The highest honour of the most eminent ministers is, to be servants of Christ. And those who are not really saints on earth, never will be saints in heaven. Out of Christ, the best saints are sinners, and unable to stand before God. There is no peace without grace. Inward peace springs from a sense of Divine favour. And there is no grace and peace but from God our Father, the fountain and origin of all blessings. At Philippi the apostle was evil entreated, and saw little fruit of his labour; yet he remembers Philippi with joy. We must thank our God for the graces and comforts, gifts and usefulness of others, as we receive the benefit, and God receives the glory. The work of grace will never be perfected till the day of Jesus Christ, the day of his appearance. But we may always be confident God will perform his good work, in every soul wherein he has really begun it by regeneration; though we must not trust in outward appearances, nor in any thing but a new creation to holiness. People are dear to their ministers, when they receive benefit by their ministry. Fellow-sufferers in the cause of God should be dear one to another.
[Phil.1.8-Phil.1.11]
Verses 8-11
Shall not we pity and love those souls whom Christ loves and pities? Those who abound in any grace, need to abound more. Try things which differ; that we may approve the things which are excellent. The truths and laws of Christ are excellent; and they recommend themselves as such to any attentive mind. Sincerity is that in which we should have our conversation in the world, and it is the glory of all our graces. Christians should not be apt to take offence, and should be very careful not to offend God or the brethren. The things which most honour God will most benefit us. Let us not leave it doubtful whether any good fruit is found in us or not. A small measure of Christian love, knowledge, and fruitfulness should not satisfy any.
[Phil.1.12-Phil.1.20]
Verses 12-20
The apostle was a prisoner at Rome; and to take off the offence of the cross, he shows the wisdom and goodness of God in his sufferings. These things made him known, where he would never have otherwise been known; and led some to inquire after the gospel. He suffered from false friends, as well as from enemies. How wretched the temper of those who preached Christ out of envy and contention, and to add affliction to the bonds that oppressed this best of men! The apostle was easy in the midst of all. Since our troubles may tend to the good of many, we ought to rejoice. Whatever turns to our salvation, is by the Spirit of Christ; and prayer is the appointed means of seeking for it. Our earnest expectation and hope should not be to be honoured of men, or to escape the cross, but to be upheld amidst temptation, contempt, and affliction. Let us leave it to Christ, which way he will make us serviceable to his glory, whether by labour or suffering, by diligence or patience, by living to his honour in working for him, or dying to his honour in suffering for him.
[Phil.1.21-Phil.1.26]
Verses 21-26
Death is a great loss to a carnal, worldly man, for he loses all his earthly comforts and all his hopes; but to a true believer it is gain, for it is the end of all his weakness and misery. It delivers him from all the evils of life, and brings him to possess the chief good. The apostle's difficulty was not between living in this world and living in heaven; between these two there is no comparison; but between serving Christ in this world and enjoying him in another. Not between two evil things, but between two good things; living to Christ and being with him. See the power of faith and of Divine grace; it can make us willing to die. In this world we are compassed with sin; but when with Christ, we shall escape sin and temptation, sorrow and death, for ever. But those who have most reason to desire to depart, should be willing to remain in the world as long as God has any work for them to do. And the more unexpected mercies are before they come, the more of God will be seen in them.
[Phil.1.27-Phil.1.30]
Verses 27-30
Those who profess the gospel of Christ, should live as becomes those who believe gospel truths, submit to gospel laws, and depend upon gospel promises. The original word "conversation" denotes the conduct of citizens who seek the credit, safety, peace, and prosperity of their city. There is that in the faith of the gospel, which is worth striving for; there is much opposition, and there is need of striving. A man may sleep and go to hell; but he who would go to heaven, must look about him and be diligent. There may be oneness of heart and affection among Christians, where there is diversity of judgment about many things. Faith is God's gift on the behalf of Christ; the ability and disposition to believe are from God. And if we suffer reproach and loss for Christ, we are to reckon them a gift, and prize them accordingly. Yet salvation must not be ascribed to bodily afflictions, as though afflictions and worldly persecutions deserved it; but from God only is salvation: faith and patience are his gifts.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesExhortations to a kind, humble spirit and behaviour.1–4The example of Christ.5–11Diligence in the affairs of salvation, and to be examples to the world.12–18The apostle's purpose of visiting Philippi.19–30
Practice Christlike humility and kindness (verses 1–4)

Paul continued calling Christians to unity of mind and a humble attitude, following the example of Jesus.

Kindness is the law of Christ's kingdom, the lesson of his school and the identifying clothing of his family.

The Lord's compassion toward us should move us to show compassion to one another.

Seeing believers live in loving agreement brings great joy to faithful ministers.

Christ humbled himself for our sake.

How inappropriate for pride to govern those who belong to him!

We should examine our own faults strictly, identifying our weaknesses quickly.

Toward others, however, we should be ready to make generous allowances.

Caring about other people does not mean becoming busybodies who interfere in every private matter.

Neither outward peace nor inward peace can endure without humility of heart.

Jesus Christ humbled himself and was exalted (verses 5–11)

Jesus Christ's example is the standard for our attitudes and behavior.

If we would receive the blessings of his death, we should seek to resemble him in life.

Henry explicitly distinguishes Christ's two natures.

In his divine nature, Jesus is the eternal, only-begotten Son who shares God's nature (John 1:1).

Equality with God was his by right, and he could rightly receive divine worship.

In his human nature, he became like us in every respect except sin.

Of his own free will he stooped from the glory he shared with the Father before the world existed.

The passage describes two states of Christ: humiliation and exaltation.

He did not merely assume a human appearance.

He entered a lowly human condition, without worldly magnificence.

His life was marked by poverty and suffering.

His deepest humiliation was dying on a cross, the death assigned to criminals and slaves, bearing public contempt and hatred.

His exaltation involved his human nature united to his divine nature.

At Jesus' name, everyone should bow—not because of the mere sound of a word, but because of the authority of Jesus himself.

Confessing Jesus Christ as Lord glorifies God the Father.

The Father wills that the Son should receive the honor rightly given to the Father (John 5:23).

What greater reason could there be for self-denying love?

Do we love and obey the Son of God in this way?

Work diligently because God is at work within you (verses 12–18)

Christians must diligently use the appointed means that lead toward salvation, persevering until the end.

We should be careful not to fall short despite our many privileges.

Work out your salvation, because God works within you.

God's action is not an excuse for laziness.

It encourages our greatest effort because we know our work, carried out by his grace, will not be wasted.

Yet in everything we must depend upon God's grace.

His gracious work within us awakens and strengthens our effort.

His favor is the reason he does such good within our souls.

Do your duties without grumbling or endless quarrelling.

Rather than constantly complaining about the work assigned, concentrate on performing it well.

Avoid giving others good reason to stumble.

God's children should be distinguishable from the world's prevailing conduct.

The more corrupt others become, the more careful we should be to remain blameless and harmless.

The teaching and example of consistent believers can light the way for others, like a lighthouse warning sailors away from rocks and guiding them safely into a harbor.

Let us shine in that way.

The gospel is the word of life, revealing eternal life through Jesus Christ.

Paul's language of running pictures energetic, determined effort.

His language of laboring pictures steadfast, careful work.

God wills that believers should rejoice often.

People blessed with faithful ministers have good reason to rejoice with them.

Timothy and Epaphroditus serve sincerely (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.19-Phil.2.30" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 19–30</reference>)

We are in a good spiritual condition when fulfilling duty becomes natural to us—meaning sincere, willing and free from pretense.

We commonly place our own reputation, comfort and safety above truth, holiness and duty.

Timothy did not.

Paul hoped for freedom from imprisonment not primarily to enjoy himself but to do good for others.

Epaphroditus wanted to return to Philippi to comfort the believers who had been distressed over his illness.

Henry thinks his illness seems to have resulted from his service to God.

Paul therefore urged the Philippians to hold him in even greater affection.

Mercies restored after we nearly lost them bring a special joy.

That is a reason to value recovered health, friendship or service more deeply.

And blessings received in answer to prayer should produce particularly sincere gratitude and rejoicing.
classic_reading:
[Phil.2.1-Phil.2.4]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Exhortations to a kind, humble spirit and behaviour.
(1-4)
The example of Christ.
(5-11)
Diligence in the affairs of salvation, and to be examples to the world.
(12-18)
The apostle's purpose of visiting Philippi.
(19-30)
Verses 1-4
Here are further exhortations to Christian duties; to like-mindedness and lowly-mindedness, according to the example of the Lord Jesus. Kindness is the law of Christ's kingdom, the lesson of his school, the livery of his family. Several motives to brotherly love are mentioned. If you expect or experience the benefit of God's compassions to yourselves, be compassionate one to another. It is the joy of ministers to see people like-minded. Christ came to humble us, let there not be among us a spirit of pride. We must be severe upon our own faults, and quick in observing our own defects, but ready to make favourable allowances for others. We must kindly care for others, but not be busy-bodies in other men's matters. Neither inward nor outward peace can be enjoyed, without lowliness of mind.
[Phil.2.5-Phil.2.11]
Verses 5-11
The example of our Lord Jesus Christ is set before us. We must resemble him in his life, if we would have the benefit of his death. Notice the two natures of Christ; his Divine nature, and human nature. Who being in the form of God, partaking the Divine nature, as the eternal and only-begotten Son of God, [John.1.1] Joh 1:1, had not thought it a robbery to be equal with God, and to receive Divine worship from men. His human nature; herein he became like us in all things except sin. Thus low, of his own will, he stooped from the glory he had with the Father before the world was. Christ's two states, of humiliation and exaltation, are noticed. Christ not only took upon him the likeness and fashion, or form of a man, but of one in a low state; not appearing in splendour. His whole life was a life of poverty and suffering. But the lowest step was his dying the death of the cross, the death of a malefactor and a slave; exposed to public hatred and scorn. The exaltation was of Christ's human nature, in union with the Divine. At the name of Jesus, not the mere sound of the word, but the authority of Jesus, all should pay solemn homage. It is to the glory of God the Father, to confess that Jesus Christ is Lord; for it is his will, that all men should honour the Son as they honour the Father, [John.5.23] Joh 5:23. Here we see such motives to self-denying love as nothing else can supply. Do we thus love and obey the Son of God?
[Phil.2.12-Phil.2.18]
Verses 12-18
We must be diligent in the use of all the means which lead to our salvation, persevering therein to the end. With great care, lest, with all our advantages, we should come short. Work out your salvation, for it is God who worketh in you. This encourages us to do our utmost, because our labour shall not be in vain: we must still depend on the grace of God. The working of God's grace in us, is to quicken and engage our endeavours. God's good-will to us, is the cause of his good work in us. Do your duty without murmurings. Do it, and do not find fault with it. Mind your work, and do not quarrel with it. By peaceableness; give no just occasion of offence. The children of God should differ from the sons of men. The more perverse others are, the more careful we should be to keep ourselves blameless and harmless. The doctrine and example of consistent believers will enlighten others, and direct their way to Christ and holiness, even as the light-house warns mariners to avoid rocks, and directs their course into the harbour. Let us try thus to shine. The gospel is the word of life, it makes known to us eternal life through Jesus Christ. Running, denotes earnestness and vigour, continual pressing forward; labouring, denotes constancy, and close application. It is the will of God that believers should be much in rejoicing; and those who are so happy as to have good ministers, have great reason to rejoice with them. ( [Phil.2.19-Phil.2.30] Php 2:19-30)
[Phil.2.19-Phil.2.30]
Verses 19-30
It is best with us, when our duty becomes natural to us. Naturally, that is, sincerely, and not in pretence only; with a willing heart and upright views. We are apt to prefer our own credit, ease, and safety, before truth, holiness, and duty; but Timothy did not so. Paul desired liberty, not that he might take pleasure, but that he might do good. Epaphroditus was willing to go to the Philippians, that he might be comforted with those who had sorrowed for him when he was sick. It seems, his illness was caused by the work of God. The apostle urges them to love him the more on that account. It is doubly pleasant to have our mercies restored by God, after great danger of their removal; and this should make them more valued. What is given in answer to prayer, should be received with great thankfulness and joy.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle cautions the Philippians against judaizing false teachers, and renounces his own former privileges.1–11Expresses earnest desire to be found in Christ; also his pressing on toward perfection; and recommends his own example to other believers.12–21
Christ's righteousness matters more than every human privilege (verses 1–11)

Sincere Christians rejoice in Jesus Christ.

The prophet referred to false prophets as silent dogs (Isaiah 56:10). Paul seems to have that language in mind when he warned against dangerous teachers. Like fierce dogs, they barked at and attacked those who faithfully professed Christ's gospel.

They insisted upon human works in opposition to faith in Jesus, but Paul called them evil workers. They were the concision, cutting apart and dividing Christ's church.

Every religious exercise is empty unless the heart is truly engaged. We worship God through the Holy Spirit's strength and grace, taking our joy in Christ rather than in merely outward practices or experiences.

We cannot guard too seriously against doctrines that oppose or misuse the gospel of free salvation.

If Paul had wanted to boast about human advantages or rely upon his own religious record, he had more reason than almost anyone to do so.

But everything he had counted as gain during his life as a Pharisee he now counted as loss because of Christ.

Paul was asking the Philippians to do nothing he had not already done, and to trust their souls to no foundation other than the One on whom he had staked his own eternal hope.

He regarded worldly possessions, religious distinctions and claims of personal merit as worthless compared with knowing Christ personally through faith in his salvation.

This was not merely an easy claim made while he still enjoyed life's comforts. Paul had actually lost everything for the privilege of belonging to Christ.

He went further. Whatever tried to rival Christ in his heart, or pretended to provide merit before God, he counted as the foulest refuse, something thrown away.

True knowledge of Christ changes a person's judgments, desires, conduct and character so deeply that the person seems to have been made anew.

It is far better to lack worldly wealth than to be without Christ and his word.

Paul therefore resolved to hold fast to Christ and heaven.

Guilty sinners need a righteousness in which they can appear before God. Christ provides that righteousness, and it is complete and perfect.

People who trust themselves cannot receive its benefit. Faith in Christ's blood is the appointed means by which we receive this saving gift.

We become conformed to his death as we die to sin, just as Christ died for sin. Through his cross, the world becomes crucified to us and we to it.

Paul was willing to act or suffer in whatever way was necessary on his path toward the glorious resurrection of believers.

This hope sustained him through all his labor and trouble.

He did not expect to attain that resurrection through his own righteousness or merit, but through the merits and righteousness of Jesus Christ.

Keep pressing forward toward Christ and heaven (verses 12–21)

Paul's sincere dependence upon Christ did not mean he had already obtained the prize or had already become perfectly like the Savior.

He refused to be satisfied with past service or his present measure of grace.

He reached forward eagerly to become more like Jesus.

A runner must not stop before finishing the race. Likewise, Christians who hope for heaven must continue pressing toward it through holy desires, confident hope and persevering effort.

Eternal life is God's gift in Jesus Christ. We cannot enter heaven as our home except through Christ, who is the Way.

Believers seek to become increasingly like him, including in suffering and death: they die to sin and crucify sinful desires.

Genuine Christians differ greatly in the progress they have made, but all experience something of this change. Christ becomes everything to them, and their hearts turn toward the world to come.

They may also differ in judgment about lesser questions.

Those differences should not cause believers to condemn one another.

They are united in Christ and expect soon to meet in heaven. Let them therefore stand together on the great truths they share and patiently await further light on less important matters.

By contrast, the enemies of Christ's cross set their minds upon sinful bodily appetites.

Sin is shameful, and is even more disgraceful when a sinner takes pride in it.

The life of those absorbed in worldly desires may seem pleasant for a time, but it ends in death and judgment. People who choose that path will share that end.

A Christian's life belongs in heaven, where Christ the Head is and where the believer's lasting home awaits.

Our citizenship and deepest affections should therefore be directed there.

Christ has also reserved glory for the bodies of his people.

At the resurrection, their bodies will not simply live again. They will be raised into a glorious condition, transformed by Christ's almighty power.

Let us be prepared for the return of our Judge.

Ask him daily to renew our souls in holiness, rescue us from spiritual enemies and make both our bodies and souls instruments of righteousness in his service.
classic_reading:
[Phil.3.1-Phil.3.11]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The apostle cautions the Philippians against judaizing false teachers, and renounces his own former privileges. | (1-11) |
Expresses earnest desire to be found in Christ; also his pressing on toward perfection; and recommends his own example to other believers. | (12-21) |
Verses 1-11
Sincere Christians rejoice in Christ Jesus. The prophet calls the false prophets dumb dogs, [Isa.56.10] Is 56:10; to which the apostle seems to refer. Dogs, for their malice against faithful professors of the gospel of Christ, barking at them and biting them. They urged human works in opposition to the faith of Christ; but Paul calls them evil-workers. He calls them the concision; as they rent the church of Christ, and cut it to pieces. The work of religion is to no purpose, unless the heart is in it, and we must worship God in the strength and grace of the Divine Spirit. They rejoice in Christ Jesus, not in mere outward enjoyments and performances. Nor can we too earnestly guard against those who oppose or abuse the doctrine of free salvation. If the apostle would have gloried and trusted in the flesh, he had as much cause as any man. But the things which he counted gain while a Pharisee, and had reckoned up, those he counted loss for Christ. The apostle did not persuade them to do any thing but what he himself did; or to venture on any thing but that on which he himself ventured his never-dying soul. He deemed all these things to be but loss, compared with the knowledge of Christ, by faith in his person and salvation. He speaks of all worldly enjoyments and outward privileges which sought a place with Christ in his heart, or could pretend to any merit and desert, and counted them but loss; but it might be said, It is easy to say so; but what would he do when he came to the trial? He had suffered the loss of all for the privileges of a Christian. Nay, he not only counted them loss, but the vilest refuse, offals thrown to dogs; not only less valuable than Christ, but in the highest degree contemptible, when set up as against him. True knowledge of Christ alters and changes men, their judgments and manners, and makes them as if made again anew. The believer prefers Christ, knowing that it is better for us to be without all worldly riches, than without Christ and his word. Let us see what the apostle resolved to cleave to, and that was Christ and heaven. We are undone, without righteousness wherein to appear before God, for we are guilty. There is a righteousness provided for us in Jesus Christ, and it is a complete and perfect righteousness. None can have benefit by it, who trust in themselves. Faith is the appointed means of applying the saving benefit. It is by faith in Christ's blood. We are made conformable to Christ's death, when we die to sin, as he died for sin; and the world is crucified to us, and we to the world, by the cross of Christ. The apostle was willing to do or to suffer any thing, to attain the glorious resurrection of saints. This hope and prospect carried him through all difficulties in his work. He did not hope to attain it through his own merit and righteousness, but through the merit and righteousness of Jesus Christ. ( [Phil.3.12-Phil.3.21] Php 3:12-21)
[Phil.3.12-Phil.3.21]
Verses 12-21
This simple dependence and earnestness of soul, were not mentioned as if the apostle had gained the prize, or were already made perfect in the Saviour's likeness. He forgot the things which were behind, so as not to be content with past labours or present measures of grace. He reached forth, stretched himself forward towards his point; expressions showing great concern to become more and more like unto Christ. He who runs a race, must never stop short of the end, but press forward as fast as he can; so those who have heaven in their view, must still press forward to it, in holy desires and hopes, and constant endeavours. Eternal life is the gift of God, but it is in Christ Jesus; through his hand it must come to us, as it is procured for us by him. There is no getting to heaven as our home, but by Christ as our Way. True believers, in seeking this assurance, as well as to glorify him, will seek more nearly to resemble his sufferings and death, by dying to sin, and by crucifying the flesh with its affections and lusts. In these things there is a great difference among real Christians, but all know something of them. Believers make Christ all in all, and set their hearts upon another world. If they differ from one another, and are not of the same judgment in lesser matters, yet they must not judge one another; while they all meet now in Christ, and hope to meet shortly in heaven. Let them join in all the great things in which they are agreed, and wait for further light as to lesser things wherein they differ. The enemies of the cross of Christ mind nothing but their sensual appetites. Sin is the sinner's shame, especially when gloried in. The way of those who mind earthly things, may seem pleasant, but death and hell are at the end of it. If we choose their way, we shall share their end. The life of a Christian is in heaven, where his Head and his home are, and where he hopes to be shortly; he sets his affections upon things above; and where his heart is, there will his conversation be. There is glory kept for the bodies of the saints, in which they will appear at the resurrection. Then the body will be made glorious; not only raised again to life, but raised to great advantage. Observe the power by which this change will be wrought. May we be always prepared for the coming of our Judge; looking to have our vile bodies changed by his Almighty power, and applying to him daily to new-create our souls unto holiness; to deliver us from our enemies, and to employ our bodies and souls as instruments of righteousness in his service.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle exhorts the Philippians to stand fast in the Lord.1Gives directions to some, and to all in general.2–9Expresses contentment in every condition of life.10–19He concludes with prayer to God the Father, and his usual blessing.20–23
Stand firm in the Lord (verse 1)

Our confident hope of eternal life should make us steadfast and constant in following Christ.

Believers have different gifts and enjoy different measures of grace. Yet all have been renewed by the same Holy Spirit, so we are brothers and sisters in Christ.

To stand firm in the Lord is to stand by his strength and grace, not our own.

Agree, rejoice and bring every concern to God (verses 2–9)

Believers should seek unity of mind and be ready to help one another.

Paul had experienced the benefit of his friends' assistance and knew how much other gospel workers would value similar help.

Let us seek sound assurance that our names are written in the book of life.

Rejoicing in the Lord is deeply important to Christian living. Believers need to be called to it again and again, because that joy outweighs every reason for sorrow.

Let opponents observe our moderation concerning outward circumstances and the calmness with which we bear losses and suffering.

The day of judgment is coming. For believers it will bring complete redemption; for the ungodly, destruction.

Not every kind of concern is wrong.

There is diligent care, which is our duty and includes wise planning and an appropriate awareness of responsibilities.

But there is also anxious, distrustful care, which is sinful, foolish and destructive to inward peace.

The appointed remedy for oppressive anxiety is constant prayer.

We should not pray only at fixed times, but turn to the Lord in everything.

Combine thanksgiving with requests. Do not merely ask for what you lack; recognize the mercies you have already received.

God knows our desires and needs better than we do. He requires prayer so that we acknowledge our dependence upon him and learn to value his gifts.

The peace of God is the comforting knowledge of reconciliation with him, a share in his favor and hope of heavenly happiness.

No words can fully express its value.

Through Jesus Christ this peace protects hearts and minds. It keeps believers from sinning under troubles or being overwhelmed by them, granting calmness and inward contentment.

Christians should seek and preserve a good reputation for virtuous conduct before God and upright people.

We should remain faithful to every kind of virtue whether or not other people praise us.

Paul's teaching and conduct agreed. He offered his own life as an example.

The way to enjoy the God of peace is to remain close to our duty.

Every privilege and the whole of our salvation come from God's free mercy, yet the enjoyment of those blessings is associated with sincere, holy conduct.

Even that obedience is God's own work within us. All praise belongs to him—not to human beings, words or deeds.

Learn contentment in poverty and prosperity (verses 10–19)

Helping a faithful minister who is suffering is a good work.

Genuine Christian sympathy does not stop at feeling sorry for people. It moves us to do what we can to help them.

Paul had often known imprisonment, poverty, hardship and physical need.

Yet through every circumstance he learned to be content—to bring his desires into agreement with the situation God appointed and to use it as well as possible.

Discontent can arise even when circumstances are favorable.

Pride, unbelief, restless desire for what we lack and sudden dissatisfaction with what we possess all contribute to it.

When brought low, we should pray for patient submission and confidence in God.

When raised to prosperity, pray for humility and a heavenly mind.

A steady, contented spirit in every circumstance is a special gift of grace.

In poverty, believers should not abandon their comfort in God, distrust his Providence or pursue unlawful means of meeting needs.

In prosperity, they must not become proud, careless or worldly.

In fact, prosperity is a harder spiritual lesson than poverty, because plenty brings greater temptations than scarcity.

Paul was not writing to pressure the Philippians for another gift.

He wanted to encourage the charitable love they had already shown, assuring them that it would receive God's reward.

Through Christ we receive grace to do what is good, and through Christ we expect the reward.

Everything we possess comes through him. Therefore we should use everything for him and his glory.

Praise the Father and receive Christ's grace (verses 20–23)

Paul closed his letter with praise to God.

Even when weakness and fear trouble us, we should look to the Lord not as an enemy but as our Father, ready to pity and help us.

Glory therefore belongs to him as Father.

God's favorable acceptance of reconciled souls, together with every gracious quality produced within them, is purchased through Christ's merit and applied through his intercession.

For this reason those blessings are rightly called the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.
classic_reading:
[Phil.4.1]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The apostle exhorts the Philippians to stand fast in the Lord. | (1) |
Gives directions to some, and to all in general. | (2-9) |
Expresses contentment in every condition of life. | (10-19) |
He concludes with prayer to God the Father, and his usual blessing. | (20-23) |
Verse 1
The believing hope and prospect of eternal life, should make us steady and constant in our Christian course. There is difference of gifts and graces, yet, being renewed by the same Spirit, we are brethren. To stand fast in the Lord, is to stand fast in his strength, and by his grace.
[Phil.4.2-Phil.4.9]
Verses 2-9
Let believers be of one mind, and ready to help each other. As the apostle had found the benefit of their assistance, he knew how comfortable it would be to his fellow-labourers to have the help of others. Let us seek to give assurance that our names are written in the book of life. Joy in God is of great consequence in the Christian life; and Christians need to be again and again called to it. It more than outweighs all causes for sorrow. Let their enemies perceive how moderate they were as to outward things, and how composedly they suffered loss and hardships. The day of judgment will soon arrive, with full redemption to believers, and destruction to ungodly men. There is a care of diligence which is our duty, and agrees with a wise forecast and due concern; but there is a care of fear and distrust, which is sin and folly, and only perplexes and distracts the mind. As a remedy against perplexing care, constant prayer is recommended. Not only stated times for prayer, but in every thing by prayer. We must join thanksgivings with prayers and supplications; not only seek supplies of good, but own the mercies we have received. God needs not to be told our wants or desires; he knows them better than we do; but he will have us show that we value the mercy, and feel our dependence on him. The peace of God, the comfortable sense of being reconciled to God, and having a part in his favour, and the hope of the heavenly blessedness, are a greater good than can be fully expressed. This peace will keep our hearts and minds through Christ Jesus; it will keep us from sinning under troubles, and from sinking under them; keep us calm and with inward satisfaction. Believers are to get and to keep a good name; a name for good things with God and good men. We should walk in all the ways of virtue, and abide therein; then, whether our praise is of men or not, it will be of God. The apostle is for an example. His doctrine and life agreed together. The way to have the God of peace with us, is to keep close to our duty. All our privileges and salvation arise in the free mercy of God; yet the enjoyment of them depends on our sincere and holy conduct. These are works of God, pertaining to God, and to him only are they to be ascribed, and to no other, neither men, words, nor deeds.
[Phil.4.10-Phil.4.19]
Verses 10-19
It is a good work to succour and help a good minister in trouble. The nature of true Christian sympathy, is not only to feel concern for our friends in their troubles, but to do what we can to help them. The apostle was often in bonds, imprisonments, and necessities; but in all, he learned to be content, to bring his mind to his condition, and make the best of it. Pride, unbelief, vain hankering after something we have not got, and fickle disrelish of present things, make men discontented even under favourable circumstances. Let us pray for patient submission and hope when we are abased; for humility and a heavenly mind when exalted. It is a special grace to have an equal temper of mind always. And in a low state not to lose our comfort in God, nor distrust his providence, nor take any wrong course for our own supply. In a prosperous condition not to be proud, or secure, or worldly. This is a harder lesson than the other; for the temptations of fulness and prosperity are more than those of affliction and want. The apostle had no design to urge them to give more, but to encourage such kindness as will meet a glorious reward hereafter. Through Christ we have grace to do what is good, and through him we must expect the reward; and as we have all things by him, let us do all things for him, and to his glory.
[Phil.4.20-Phil.4.23]
Verses 20-23
The apostle ends with praises to God. We should look upon God, under all our weakness and fears, not as an enemy, but as a Father, disposed to pity us and help us. We must give glory to God as a Father. God's grace and favour, which reconciled souls enjoy, with the whole of the graces in us, which flow from it, are all purchased for us by Christ's merit, and applied by his pleading for us; and therefore are justly called the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.
